content: The use of multiple technologies and fuels in households is common for various purposes such as cooking, heating, lighting, boiling water, bathing, washing clothes, and food processing. Research consistently shows that new technologies and fuels are often integrated into existing practices rather than completely replacing older methods, at least in the short term. This pattern is expected to apply to transitions in fuels and technologies used for heating and lighting as well. Where solid fuel technologies remain necessary, the lowest-emission options that meet household needs, safety, and cost considerations should be developed and promoted. For households relying on improved solid fuel stoves as an interim solution, efforts should be made to prepare for the transition to clean fuels as soon as possible. When evaluating alternative technologies and fuels, factors such as acceptability, costs, emissions, and safety must be considered. The World Health Organization (WHO) supports the development of tools to assist in these assessments, including enhanced emissions models and intervention assessment tools. Transitioning from traditional solid fuels to low-emission stoves, clean fuels, or electricity varies across different social and geographic groups. For example, in rural Mexico, households may use a combination of wood-fired stoves and liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) stoves. This fuel stacking highlights the complexity of achieving exclusive use of clean technologies. The effectiveness of any stove or fuel in reducing emissions depends on its consistent and sustained use. Factors influencing the adoption and long-term use of improved stoves and clean fuels include household characteristics, financial considerations, market development, regulations, and programmatic mechanisms. Maintenance and replacement of equipment are also critical for sustained use. Research is needed to address knowledge gaps, such as the health impacts of kerosene use, the role of black carbon, and factors influencing sustained adoption of clean technologies. Studies on the real-life effectiveness of improved household energy technologies and clean fuels are crucial for understanding their cost-effectiveness and health benefits. The WHO guidelines on household fuel combustion will be updated periodically based on new evidence. This includes updates to air quality guidelines for specific pollutants and emissions models. The development of interactive tools for region-specific data input is also recommended to enhance the practical application of these guidelines. Finally, the implementation of these guidelines requires robust systems for testing and standardization, particularly in regions where they are most needed. WHO collaborates with international partners to develop and enforce standards for household energy technologies, ensuring their alignment with health-based evidence.
